content: The WHO STI team reviewed the declarations of interest (DOI) of all members involved in the guideline development process. After thorough analysis, it was determined that no member had financial or commercial interests related to STI treatment. Any other declared interests were minor, either unrelated to STI or associated with non-commercial grants or interests. The team concluded that there were no significant conflicts of interest that would prevent any member from fully participating in the guideline development process. The WHO STI guidelines make two types of recommendations: strong recommendations, indicated by the phrase The WHO STI guideline recommends, and conditional recommendations, indicated by the phrase The WHO STI guideline suggests. For patients, most individuals in the relevant situations would prefer the recommended course of action, with only a small proportion opting otherwise. For clinicians, the majority of individuals should receive the recommended course of action. However, clinicians must recognize that different choices may be appropriate for different individuals and should assist patients in making decisions consistent with their values and preferences. Decision aids may be helpful in this regard. Policymaking will require substantial debate and the involvement of various stakeholders. The guidelines will be disseminated through multiple channels, including printed publications, downloads from the WHO Department of Reproductive Health and Research website, and inclusion in the WHO Reproductive Health Library. They will also be available in a guideline application created with the GRADEpro GDT software. Announcements will be made in newsletters from the WHO and other relevant organizations. WHO headquarters will collaborate with regional and country offices to support countries in adapting, implementing, and monitoring the guidelines. This will involve working with partners such as UNFPA, UNICEF, UNAIDS, NGOs, and other agencies to integrate the recommendations into sexual and reproductive health, family planning, and maternal, neonatal, child, and adolescent health services. A system for monitoring new evidence and updating the recommendations will be established within a year of guideline implementation. An electronic follow-up survey of key end-users will be conducted to identify challenges, barriers, and gaps in the guidelines, as well as to evaluate their usefulness in improving service delivery. The guidelines for the treatment of gonorrhea are based on the best global evidence available at the time of compilation. However, the epidemiology and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) of STIs vary by location and change over time. Countries are encouraged to conduct high-quality studies to adapt the guidelines to their local STI situation. In the absence of local data, the recommendations can be adopted as presented. The selection of medications should prioritize high efficacy (at least 95% cure rate), low cost, low toxicity, and minimal likelihood of resistance development. Medications should also be suitable for oral administration, single-dose regimens, and use in pregnant or lactating women. Quantifying medication needs is critical for budgeting and ensuring an adequate supply. National programs should consider joint procurement schemes to reduce costs and place STI medications on essential medicines lists to increase accessibility. Key populations, such as sex workers, men who have sex with men, transgender persons, and people living with HIV, are at increased risk of transmitting and acquiring STIs, including gonorrhea. It is essential to increase access to STI services for these groups. WHO guidelines provide recommendations for delivering comprehensive HIV/STI programs tailored to key populations. For the treatment of gonococcal infections, the WHO recommends that local resistance data guide the choice of therapy. In settings without local resistance data, dual therapy is suggested over single therapy. Dual therapy options include ceftriaxone 250 mg intramuscularly plus azithromycin 1 g orally, or cefixime 400 mg orally plus azithromycin 1 g orally. Single therapy options, based on local resistance data, include ceftriaxone 250 mg IM, cefixime 400 mg orally, or spectinomycin 2 g IM. Due to emerging resistance, quinolones are no longer recommended. The evidence for dual versus single therapy is of low quality, but dual therapy is favored due to resistance concerns and the lack of local surveillance data in many regions. For pregnant women, the evidence for the effects of treatments for gonococcal infections is limited. Recommendations are informed by evidence from non-pregnant adults when data for pregnant women are unavailable. Dual therapy is preferred over single therapy due to emerging resistance and the need for effective treatment options. The WHO emphasizes the importance of local surveillance data to guide treatment decisions and recommends further studies to evaluate different combinations of dual therapy. Injectable medications may be less desirable for some patients and healthcare providers due to acceptability and resource considerations. However, dual therapy is generally acceptable and cost-effective compared to single therapy.
